title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Regression
claim: Standard robust and empirical baselines suffer regret that grows with dimension or misspecified radius, while the proposed methods stay near zero.
layout: 2 line-plot panels side by side; solid vs dashed curves, vertical reference line
description: Two line plots side by side, both with population regret on the y-axis. The left panel, Setting A, plots regret against dimension d from about 20 to 400. ERM (orange-red) and DRO (yellow) climb steadily to roughly 8, while MRO (blue) and SNR (green) stay flat near zero. The right panel, Setting B, plots regret against supplied radius ρ on a log axis from 10^-1 to about 20. ERM is flat near 8. DRO dips slightly, then rises sharply to about 75. SNR and MRO fall to near zero across a wide middle range. SNR then explodes to about 90 at large radius, and MRO jumps only at the far right. Solid lines show finite-sample results and dashed lines show population benchmarks. A gray dashed vertical line marks the true budget at ρ=1. A legend sits in the left panel.
caption: Target population regret R( ˆA[Ps,n], P) for Settings A (left) and B (right). Solid curves show finite-sample averages, while dashed curves show population benchmarks. For Setting B, the dashed vertical line marks the corruption budget ε = 1.
abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $Îº$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(Îº\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.
